newsitem.title: USA: US 30-yr mortgage rate falls 7th consecutive week.
newsitem.headline: US 30-yr mortgage rate falls 7th consecutive week.

text.p: The average interest rate on U.S. 30-year fixed-rate mortgages fell to 7.44 percent in the week ending December 6, a seventh consecutive weekly decline, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp said Thursday.
Freddie Mac said the 30-year has not been lower since the week ended March 8, 1996, when the average was 7.38 percent. Last week's 30-year rate was 7.52 percent.
Fifteen-year loans also fell a seventh consecutive week to an average 6.96 percent, the lowest since a rate of 6.87 percent in the March 8 week. Last week's 15-year rate averaged 7.04 percent.
Adjustable rate mortgages inched down to an average 5.47 percent from 5.50 percent last week. The ARM has not been lower since it stood at 5.40 percent in the March 8 week, Freddie Mac said.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.18 percent, the 15-year 6.74 percent, and the ARM 5.53 percent.
"Interest rates today rival those of the early 1970s," Robert Van Order, Freddie Mac chief economist, said.

"Economic signs of little or no inflation, coupled with a steady, sustainable rate of growth have encouraged the decline in interest rates that we have seen over the last seven weeks," Van Order added.

On Tuesday the Conference Board said U.S. October leading indicators rose 0.1 percent while the Commerce Department reported an 8.7 percent decline in sales of U.S. October single-family homes to a 714,000-unit annualized rate.
On Friday the Labor Department will issue U.S. employment data for November.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30-year loans, down from 1.8 percent last week. They charged 1.7 percent on 15-year loans, unchanged from the previous week, and 1.3 percent on the ARM, down from 1.4 percent last week.
